newsitem.title: RUSSIA: London Club deal seen cutting Russia T-bill yields.
newsitem.headline: London Club deal seen cutting Russia T-bill yields.

text.p: Progress towards a rescheduling of billions of dollars of Russia's Soviet-era debt is likely to help push down Treasury bill yields, though no big fall is in prospect, analysts said.

Russia said last week that commercial banks had agreed in principle to reschedule more than $20 billion in debt, paving the way for a deal rescheduling all the $35 billion Russia owes the London Club of banks and for a long-awaited Eurobond issue.

Russian Vneshekonombank external debt and Ministry of Finance bonds, known as MinFins, rose sharply after Deputy Finance Minister Mikhail Kasyanov said the so-called "critical mass" needed to ensure a rescheduling deal had been reached.
Dollar-denominated debt RUVNUSLNS=RR was at 69.625 bid late on Wednesday after opening at 70.000. Early last week it was around 62.
But some analysts said the prospects of a London Club deal would also have an impact in the market for rouble instruments such as GKO discount Treasury bills.

"You might see more (foreign) interest in investing in GKOs. It will not be as direct an effect as in MinFins but there certainly will be an effect in terms of pulling yields down," said Peter Kisler, fixed income analyst with Rinaco-Plus.
An auction of six-month bills on Wednesday yielded an average 61.25 percent, down from 67.97 percent on September 11.
Bills with three months to maturity are yielding about 45 percent. The government has said it wants to cut T-bill yields to 20-50 percent, depending on maturity, by year-end.

United City Bank said in a monthly fixed income outlook, published before the debt rescheduling announcement, that it expected average yields of 60-73 percent in September with a further fall towards 50 percent by the end of the year.
But it said a further decrease in yields would depend on large foreign capital inflows to the market.

Alliance-Menatep fixed income trader and analyst Dmitry Falkovich said prospects of a London Club deal would have a positive impact on investor attitudes to Russia but that there would be a fundamental change once Moscow's access to international borrowing was increased next year.
"It will have a slight effect because the general investor attitude to Russia will be a little bit more favourable.
"But in terms of fundamentals, in terms of the capital that Russia will be able to raise and substitute internal funding, that is not substantial," he said.

Russia recently eased access to the government securities market for non-residents. The real dollar yield for foreigners has been capped at 19 percent via forward deals, of a minimum three months, necessary to repatriate the proceeds.

However, analysts say foreigners can increase the yield to around 30 percent. Non-residents will receive 19 percent only if they hold three-month bills to maturity. If they invested over a longer period, the dollar yield would be greater.

Kisler said that as the market developed, investors would increasingly switch between T-bills and the longer-term instruments. "Once investors are effectively able to hedge GKOs, you are going to see people moving back and forth," he said.
However, Robert Devane, head of fixed income at Troika-Dialog, said investors in domestic fixed income had different concerns from those interested in long-term debt.
He said foreigners who had invested in T-bills were "pretty risk-prone" and were attracted by the yields.
Investors in Russian T-bills face currency, counterparty and settlement risks which will not affect investors in the Eurobond.
Devane did not see yields falling quickly. "I do not think they should be coming down any time soon simply because there isn't tremendous foreign interest even at 19 percent."
